resources.string: Show or hide the details of this tip.
Prefer val for values that never change and use var only when you really need to reassign. Immutable code is easier to reason about.
Kotlin infers types from the assigned value, so you can write val name = \"Kai\" instead of repeating the type yourself.
Embed variables directly in text with $name or compute expressions with ${a + b}. No more string concatenation.
A type like String? may hold null, while String never can. The compiler forces you to deal with it before it crashes your app.
Use ?. to call a method only when the receiver is not null. If it is null the whole expression simply evaluates to null.
Provide a fallback with ?: , for example val length = text?.length ?: 0. Short and very readable.
when replaces long if-else chains, works with ranges and types, and can return a value directly.
Write 1..10 for an inclusive range, 1 until 10 to exclude the end, and step or downTo to control the direction of a loop.
Give parameters default values to avoid writing many overloads. Callers only pass what they want to change.
Call functions with names such as createUser(name = \"Kai\", age = 20). The code documents itself and the order stops mattering.
Add data in front of class and Kotlin generates equals, hashCode, toString and copy for you. Perfect for models.
When a function is one expression, drop the braces: fun square(x: Int) = x * x.
Add new functions to existing classes without inheriting from them, such as fun String.shout() = uppercase() + \"!\".
listOf and mapOf create read-only collections. Use mutableListOf and mutableMapOf when you need to change them.
A lambda is a function you can pass around. The last lambda argument can be written outside the parentheses.
Transform and select items with map and filter instead of manual loops. Chain them to build small pipelines.
Use forEach for simple iteration and withIndex or forEachIndexed when you also need the position of every item.
let runs a block on a non-null object: name?.let { println(it) }. It is a neat way to unwrap nullable values.
apply configures an object and returns it, which is ideal for setting several properties right after creating it.
Functions can take other functions as parameters or return them, which lets you build flexible reusable helpers.
An interface describes what a class can do. A class may implement many interfaces, and interfaces can have default method bodies.
A sealed class restricts its subclasses, so when can check every case and the compiler warns you if you forget one.
Use object for a singleton and companion object for members that belong to the class rather than to an instance.
Generics let one class or function work with many types safely, like List<T> works for strings, numbers or your own models.
In Compose, remember keeps a value across recompositions and mutableStateOf makes the UI update when the value changes.
Modifiers decorate and arrange composables. Their order matters: padding before background is not the same as after.
LazyColumn only composes the items that are visible on screen, so long lists stay smooth and use little memory.
Define colors, typography and shapes once in your theme and let every Material component follow them consistently.
Small animations such as animateContentSize or animateColorAsState explain changes to the user and make the app feel polished.
You finished the month. Build small apps, read other people\'s code and keep experimenting. Consistency beats talent.
